blocks.text: Fine-tuning a 70 billion parameter model is a common enough scenario, and a common enough interview question, that it deserves its own dedicated walkthrough pulling together the method, infrastructure, and planning decisions covered across this course into one concrete scenario.

The short answer is that the method choice, QLoRA versus full fine-tuning, determines almost everything else about the infrastructure needed, this topic walks through that decision and its consequences step by step.
1. The First Decision: Full Fine-Tuning or PEFT

blocks.alt: A 70B parameter model faces a decision between full fine-tuning and QLoRA

blocks.text: The single most consequential decision for fine-tuning a model this large is whether to use full fine-tuning or a parameter-efficient method like QLoRA, covered in earlier modules, this choice determines whether the project needs a large multi-GPU cluster or can potentially run on a single capable GPU.
2. QLoRA Makes a Single GPU Plausible

blocks.alt: QLoRA on a 70B model can fit on one high memory GPU

blocks.text: Using QLoRA, covered in the earlier LoRA vs QLoRA topic, quantizes the 70 billion frozen base weights down to 4-bit, combined with the memory estimation approach covered in the previous How Much GPU Is Needed topic, this can bring total memory needs down to a level that fits on a single high-memory GPU, a dramatically different infrastructure story than full fine-tuning.
3. Full Fine-Tuning Needs Distributed Infrastructure

blocks.alt: Full fine-tuning a 70B model requires multiple GPUs and a distributed training strategy

blocks.text: Full fine-tuning all 70 billion parameters, including their full-precision optimizer states, covered in the previous topic as often the largest memory component, essentially requires the distributed training techniques covered in an earlier module, spreading the model and its training state across multiple GPUs.

blocks.text: 4. Choosing a Distributed Strategy for Full Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 3, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism are distributed strategy options

blocks.text: If full fine-tuning is genuinely needed, DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 3, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, all covered in the earlier Distributed Training Techniques module, each offer different tradeoffs, ZeRO stage 3 is often the most straightforward starting point, sharding optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across available GPUs.
5. Reducing Activation Memory

Regardless of the method chosen, gradient checkpointing, covered in an earlier module, trades some recomputation time for a significant reduction in activation memory, a technique worth applying by default at this scale, where every gigabyte of memory saved directly affects whether the training run fits at all.

blocks.title: Activation memory is easy to underestimate at this scale
blocks.content: With a 70 billion parameter model, even a modest batch size and long sequence length can produce activation memory that rivals the model weights themselves, gradient checkpointing is close to essential rather than optional at this scale.

blocks.text: 6. Validating the Approach at Small Scale First

blocks.alt: A small scale experiment first is compared against jumping straight to a full 70B run

blocks.text: Before committing significant compute budget to the full 70 billion parameter run, validating the training pipeline, data formatting, hyperparameters, evaluation setup, on a much smaller model first catches configuration bugs cheaply, a mistake found on a small model costs minutes, the same mistake found partway through a large run can cost a substantial amount of wasted compute.
7. Estimating Cost and Time Upfront

blocks.alt: A compute cost estimate and training time estimate together inform the budget decision

blocks.text: Given the significant expense of fine-tuning a model this size, connecting to the cost optimization concerns covered in an earlier topic, estimating total compute cost and expected training time upfront, based on the chosen method and hardware, is an essential planning step before committing to the full run.
8. Data and Evaluation Considerations at This Scale

A model this large benefits from correspondingly careful data curation, covered throughout the dataset preparation modules earlier in this course, since a large compute investment amplifies the cost of training on poor quality data, evaluation, covered in an earlier module, should be planned with the same rigor given how expensive it is to discover a problem only after the full run completes.
9. Deployment Planning Should Start Early

Given the model size, deployment considerations, covered in the earlier Inference and Serving module, quantization for serving, adapter merging or loading, choice of serving framework, are worth planning alongside the training approach rather than as an afterthought, since they directly affect what training-time decisions, like using QLoRA versus full fine-tuning, make sense.
Worked Example

A team needs to fine-tune a 70 billion parameter model but has access to only a single high-memory GPU rather than a multi-GPU cluster, they choose QLoRA specifically because it makes this feasible, validating their full training pipeline, data formatting and hyperparameters, on a much smaller model first to catch any configuration issues cheaply.

Once validated, they run the actual 70B QLoRA fine-tuning job with gradient checkpointing enabled to control activation memory, and plan their deployment approach, likely serving through adapter loading rather than merging, covered in earlier topics, before the training run even completes.
Common Mistakes

items: Committing to full fine-tuning at this scale without first confirming a distributed infrastructure and budget can actually support it
Skipping small-scale pipeline validation and discovering a configuration bug only partway through the full expensive run
Not enabling gradient checkpointing, running into avoidable out-of-memory errors from activation memory at this scale
Leaving deployment planning until after training completes, missing an opportunity to make training-time decisions that ease deployment

blocks.text: Practice

For a hypothetical 70 billion parameter fine-tuning project with a single high-memory GPU available, walk through the method decision, infrastructure implications, and validation approach covered in this topic, and explain what would change in your plan if a multi-GPU cluster were available instead.
Key Takeaway

Fine-tuning a 70 billion parameter model starts with the full fine-tuning versus QLoRA decision, which determines whether a single GPU or a distributed multi-GPU setup is needed, and success at this scale depends on validating the pipeline at small scale first, applying gradient checkpointing to control activation memory, and planning deployment alongside training rather than as an afterthought, given how expensive mistakes become at this scale.
